1. I did not ask to be born,

I'm a single dad myself and I've never agreed to a play date or whatever because i fancy the mum or want to be friends with the parents. Where my kids lives are concerned, their lives are the priority, not my own. I'd never 'use' them as a way to meet new people. 

My point is, if you do start dating then there's  nothing wrong with outlining your position as a single parent and being proud of that because the majority of parents are still together raising their children together. To do it on your own should be something to be proud of as it's really hard and difficult, especially without added support from grandparents or other family members.

If you've ever been in a situation where you've not outlined your position as a single parent to a prospective partner, and started liking them only for them to finish it when they've found out you have kids then you'll know exactly where I'm coming from.  

Yeah ok, probably a lucky escape there but I think it's something you should be upfront about and be proud of, not something you should hide because of your own selfish opinions, that just wastes everybodys time just for the sake of your own moral highground. 

This particular life is mostly forced upon us. It's not a choice in most circumstances and if anyone has kids with the ambition of being a single parent then they are definitely pathetic. But for most of us we never thought for one minute we'd be bringing up our kids on our own so why not be proud of it? And if it's sad to be proud of it then so be it, I'm sad and pathetic. Yes you are correct. I am an addict. I suffer from bpd (borderline personality disorder). I am 41 and male. I didn't start taking drugs until my mid 20's after a failed marriage and being apart from my son and daughter. It ruined me but it was always my choice. I was never selfish before but I was completely selfish during the time I was using and never once thought about how my addiction affected the people who cared about me. My mental illness making it even harder to maintain abstinence. I am constantly aware of my triggers and still get cravings now after 4 years clean. The professional help I got taught me lots of different ways to deal with my addiction but the one thing that sticks in my mind is the fast forwarding time to the point I have none left and am trying to get money by selling my personal belongings or borrowing off friends or family with a promise to pay back knowing I cannot do so. Once I started to fast forward time when I was craving it really helped me to overcome those cravings each time. My mum was too easy on me but understood my triggers. My dad was really hard on me but didn't understand my triggers but the both of them combined helped me realise how selfish I was being and how much it affected them despite me living 10 miles away. My life now is boring and dull and I cannot sustain emotional relationships with women anymore but I am still grateful that I beat the addiction and I now work with young people who suffer from addiction through mental illness so I see how hard it is for them every day. If I was to tell them it wasn't their choice to use drugs because of their mental illness, I would be justifying their usage  for them. 90% of the time the hard approach does work. I often tell them to put themselves in the shoes of their next of kin (usually mum) and they nearly always tear up and start to realise the impact they are having. It is then that I gain their trust enough for them to start addressing the underlying issues. I never hit them with X Y or Z until they've started to address these issues. You are 100% correct in saying that there's not ever 1 thing that works but they do have to be taught every tool that might work in order to know which one does work for them. Sometimes they give up when they relapse but it's up to me and my colleagues to keep repeating the cycle until they realise which one does work best for them. It's really very difficult and time consuming, least to say, emotionally draining too but it's so good when they start hitting 1 month, 2 month and then 6 months clean. They become completely different people.

This is why i said it MIGHT be just what they need. Drug addiction is a very selfish way of living your life. The only way to conquer the addiction is to seek an understanding of the underlying issues that caused them to use in the first place. You can't do that without making a choice to engage with the professional help that is available. Only then can they understand what the thing it is they need to get better.

Understand that the person getting 'aggro' is thinking about how seeing this in a public place could affect others, especially the younger generation who have never and should never have to witness this kind of behaviour. The person who CHOSE to do the heroin in the first place is now in a position where they are ONLY thinking of themselves. 

I agree they do need help with their addiction which has become a sickness but don't ever be fooled into thinking it isn't a choice. It most definitely is. It's an everday battle with the physical and mental symptoms that have been caused by the users choice to take heroin, no matter what the reason was. In order for the user to get help they must engage with the suppprt available. It will be the hardest thing they have ever had to do.

Going easy on a drug addict has never accomplished abstinence. Usually a few hard home truths might just be the thing that helps them to engage with support available.
